Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock), I beg to move that the House go into Committee of the Whole on Tuesday next to consider the following proposed resolution which stands in his name:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confirm a certain Draft Convention fixing the minimum age for the admission of young persons to employment as trimmers or stokers, adopted at Geneva on the 11th day of November, 1921, by a General Conference of the International Labour Organization
of the League of Nations; to provide that any persons under the age of 18 years shall not be employed or work as trimmers or stokers on vessels engaged in maritime navigation excluding ships of war, vessels mainly propelled by other means than steam, and school ships, or training ships.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance) :
speechtext:
The hon. member for West York
(Sir Henry Drayton) on Friday evening made

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
some constructive suggestions regarding the administration of the sales tax. He pointed out that in a return tabled at a previous session, it had been stated that 3,170 firms were in arrears. I have had the officers of the department go carefully through the records, and I am now in a position to say to my hon. friend that a large number, probably 50 per cent, were in arrears under 'the 1920 act, and a large proportion of the balance of those cases arose under the 1922 act, which, for administrative purposes, was the same as the 1921 act. When we consider the amount of revenue collected, namely, over $100,000,000 in 1923-24, the outstanding items are not unduly large and no trouble in their ultimate adjustment is anticipated.
The proposed resolutions now before the committee provide that all wholesalers may be granted a license on an equal footing. The resolutions do away with the exemption from license of manufacturers of goods under $10,000 per annum. This is designed to protect further the revenue and also to protect large manufacturers against unfair competition by smaller manufacturers, which competition in some cases in the aggregate, is considerable.
The hon. member also referred to subsection 9 respecting the refund on goods imported free of duty. The purpose of this subsection is to protect a manufacturer who imports raw materials in respect of which, on the sale by the manufacturer, the freight paid would be included in the value on which sales tax had been paid. The discrimination *would be in the case of an importer of a like finished product the freight on which would not be included in the value for sales purposes.
The hon. member also stated that wholesalers are divided into two categories- licensed and unlicensed. The new resolutions provide that all wholesalers may now be licensed. The object of this change is to simplify the administration by reducing the numerous cases of refunds to which my hon. friend very correctly referred as involving private and public expense.
The purpose of paragraph B of section 12 to which the hon. member also referred, is to facilitate the securing of refunds. Under the proposed resolutions any wholesaler may take out a license, and to this extent paragraph B will be applicable. Deductions of sales tax on goods on hand on January 1, 1924, will be all disposed of by June 30, 1924. These refund claims have already been largely *disposed of.
[Mr. Kobb.l
My hon. friend referred to subsection 13 which provided that the minister may determine the value for the tax in circumstances where it is difficult to determine the value otherwise. This section deals with a very restricted class of cases, and it is modelled upon section 46 of the Customs Act which has been in existence since 1888.

What machinery has the government for seeing that everybody pays sales tax who should pay it? I would also like to refer to a remark made by the hon. member for West York on Friday last, a remark with which I thoroughly agree. There does not seem to be any very sound principle on which this sales tax is based. I interjected

Ways and Means-Sales Tax

on Friday last that I did not think there ever was any sound basis for a sales tax. I have always objected to it, and the discussion today has only confirmed my conviction that this tax is not based on any sound principle. It would be impossible for the government to see that everybody pays this tax who should pay it, without maintaining costly and cumbersome machinery. It is evidently quite hard for them to make an audit and find how much sales tax is outstanding. The sales tax is based on consumption, certainly. Now I think we wdl all agree that in order to prosper we must facilitate business in every way possible, but the sales tax, to my mind, is a clog on the wheels of industry. It is a fine on every one who attempts to do business in the commodities that bear the tax. The sound principle is to tax a man on what he is worth, and not on what he consumes. I would even be willing to do away with the exemptions in regard to income tax, and tax even small incomes a slight amount, with very sharp gradations in the tax as the incomes become greater. I think that is the only sound way in which to raise taxation. Take a poor labourer with ten children-and it is usually the poor man who has a large family; I do not know just what the reason is, but that is usually the fact-he is paying an equal amount on the goods he consumes as the millionaire, which I think every one will admit is not a sound principle. Then, take different classes and different occupations. Some occupations are buying far more goods bearing a sales tax than others. Take the farmer, for instance. Previous to this budget-he had to pay sales tax on a large amount of the equipment necessary in his business. Compare him with a city lawyer, whose only equipment is his books.

tax, because, I think, he Realized it meant an immense tax on the man who was using fertilizer. I would like to go further and refer to the soldier settler, who has had a very hard struggle to stay on the land, and a great many of whom have already left. I have a small amendment
which I desire to move, but before doing so I want to direct the attention of the minister to the enormous saving it would have been of trouble to hon. gentlemen if the information which he has just given us had been printed in his Ways and Means resolutions. For instance, he read just now section 219a and intimated in brackets so to speak, to what articles of goods it referred, and so on. It took me an hour the other day to trace all these different items out of the tariff and write their contents down in the margin of my paper, which now looks as though it had been walked over by a drunken chicken. Two hundred members had to do the same thing, or else come to this House and remain in ignorance of what was being discussed. Some of us have not got the tariff, and some of us who have got the tariff have not an up-to-date copy. The simple addition of a few words in each case would enormously have facilitated the passing of this resolution.
The amendment I want to move is only a small one. It is to insert before the word "poultry" on the tenth line the words: "Calf, cattle, hog or." The effect will be to add these to the exemption from the sales tax and the line will then read: "Calf, cattle, hog or poultry feed." At present only poultry feed is proposed to be exempted. The change I propose would simply make the exemption consistent with the policy of the government in regard to the exemption of poultry feed. I might explain that prior to the introduction of this budget both poultry and hog, cattle or calf meal were in this position. The exemption of this class of goods under the sales tax was as follows:
Bran, shorts, middlings, alfalfa meal; oil cake, oil cake meal; grains mixed or crushed for cattle or poultry feed; hay; molasses; salt-
And some other things. It will be observed that only "grains mixed' or crushed for cattle or poultry feed" are exempt. If anything is added to make the feed more 
palatable or useful, such as beef scraps or clam shells, or even linseed meal, which is not taxable in itself, yet the addition of that something different from "grains mixed or crushed" render the whole business taxable, although the addition might be a very trivial amount, perhaps only two per cent, and something that was not in itself taxable. The result was that this encouraged the usual methods of evasion, and large poultry people tried to mix their own feeds, which was not always satisfactory, and the smaller poultry people were at a great disadvantage because they had not the facilities for proper mixing. This occasioned a great deal of discontent in the trade. It is certain that some of the big companies handling poultry feed paid no attention to the regulations and tried to evade the law, in many cases successfully, whereas the honest dealers paid the tax. The ease with which it could be evaded must have made it difficult for the officials of the Finance department to collect the tax. The government appear to have been advised of these troubles, and in the resolutions they have struck the sales tax off poultry feed entirely, so that even if it contains something other than "grains mixed or crushed" it will not be liable for sales tax.
All my amendment does is to extend the exemption to calf, cattle and' hog mixtures. I am no advocate of any patent stock feeds, and the farming members will endorse my statement that the average patent stock feed is often not a very economical proposition. But calf meal is in a class entirely by itself. It must contain other ingredients than grains mixed or crushed, and it is a very essential feed nowadays in the dairy industry. Practically that industry could not be carried on to its full extent without this feed, and there is no reason why calf meal should have to pay this tax when poultry and other feeds do not.
Again, take the case of hog feed; where tankage is available it is added to bran, shorts and barley meal; but if so, then the	whole	mixture has to pay	thesales tax.	This,	I submit,	is against common sense. The	tax also applies if	molasses is	added,	although	molasses is	not
taxed in itself. The same thing happens with oil cake meal, and even if common or garden salt is added the whole mixture will have to pay the sales tax. The government,
I submit very properly, changed the regulation as regards poultry feed, thus preventing endless disputes, and without sustaining any great loss of revenue. I think the situation is parallel as regards calf, cattle or hog feed and poultry feed; it is illogical to change

the regulation in one case and not in the other. I submit it is only logical to put both of these branches of agriculture on the same footing as would be done by the adoption of this simple amendment.

5 p.m. public $4 or $5 extra and on that account certain reservations were made. But for administrative purposes I agree with my hon. friend that there is room for clearing up this apparent discrimination.
Amendment agreed to.

I note that in the resolutions tabled on April 10 in the twelfth line of paragraph 2 these words appear:
Carbolic or heavy oil, to be used only in creosoting timber.
Then in the amendment tabled on the 30th in paragraph 2 these words were changed to:
Carbolic or heavy oil, to be used only in creosoting logs and round unmanufactured timber.
Those items were to be free from the sales tax. Then at the end of the paragraph under the 2^ per cent clause the words are added, [DOT]'creosoted railway ties." What was the reason ror the change? As far as I can see it, carbolic or heavy oil to be used only in creosoting timber would cover every form of creosoting. Why are railway ties to be subject to the sales tax if creosoted, while other creosoted timber is to be free?

This correction was made to
meet a condition in eastern Canada where there were some long contracts extending over a period of ten years, and the contractor claimed he would be discriminated against unless we made this concession. The creosoted timber as originally put in remains. I know what my hon. friend has in mind, the case on the coast. The creosote is free as applied to logs on the coast.

I understand that, but this is what I want to point out: A very large percentage of the output of the coast firm is devoted to creosoting railway ties, as well as the timber. Now under the original resolution tabled on the 10th of April, all timber, whether railway ties, piling, or otherwise, would be free of the sales tax if creosoted; in other words, railway ties under the original resolution, were free from the sales tax.
No. I am told that in the department administering it they had some doubt as to that.

They have removed the
doubt all right by making it taxable. What I want to point out to the minister is this: Railway ties under the Customs Tariff Act come under the very category as the items named in his original resolution. I would like him to refer to tariff item 500, and then check that with his original resolution. Item 500 says:
Logs and round unmanufactured timber .... and railway ties.	#
Item 503 says:
Planks . . . .and other timber, not further manufactured than sawn or split, whether creosoted, vulcanized, or treated by any other preserving process, or not.
I submit that the original resolution as drawn would cover everything that was creosoted if it was timber. Therefore, the effect of the original resolution, I submit, was to remove the sales tax from railway ties, and in any case I am certain the minister had in his mind the removal of the sales tax from railway ties as well as from piling and other types of creosoted timber, I have pointed out to the minister and to his expert before on numerous occasions, and I would like to point out to both of them again, the frightful situation that has existed in this particular industry. There is nearly $400,000 of capital invested in it. All these articles come in from the United States free of customs duty. Now 50 per cent of the value of the finished prooduct consists of the raw creosote.
That is made free.

No, the creosoted railway
ties are not made free, nor square timber. I submit they should all be made free of sales tax, because they come in from the United States free of customs duty, and 50 per cent of the value of the products consists of the raw creosote. Now if the raw creosote going into railway ties is still to be assessed 2i per cent sales tax-I am not quite clear as to just what the minister now suggests-but if all creosoted railway ties are to be subjected to 2J per cent sales tax, that will be even worse; it will increase the discrimination still more.
It was 5 per cent before.

Last year the sales tax was
assessed at 6 per cent on the raw creosote only, not on the finished piling. Now, had the sales tax been assessed at 6 per cent on the finished article, that would have been the very same thing as giving a bounty of 6

Yes. Now the American manufacturer of creosoted timber, all classes of timber and planking, can ship his product

in free of duty. We have asked as a compensating feature for the Canadian manufacturer, in the absence of the duty, that he should have his heavy oil, his carbolic or creosoting oil that enters into the manufacture of these articles, exempt from the sales tax. That is our request. Now, here is what the minister gives us. He gives us:
Carbolic or heavy oil to be used only in creosoting logs and round unmanufactured timber.
That is really limiting it to piling, or, I suppose, poles. I say the wording means that logs, or really piling comes in free or rather the creosote to be used for treating them comes in free. But creosote used for bridge timbers, ties, or anything else than round unmanufactured logs, will have to pay the sales tax, whereas the American manufactured articles under this item which I have just read enter free. Now, our argument has been all along-first, that this timber is really manufactured when it goes through the process of creosoting, because the creosoting is half the value of the timber. We claim that is a process of manufacturing, and that it ought to come in under a tariff item, and that there should be some protection in that regard, but such is not granted under the law. We claim as a result of this the American producer of creosoted timber has an advantage over the Canadian manufacturer of creosoted timber to the extent of the sales tax on the creosote or oil that goes into that timber, and that equals about half the price of the product. In other words it amounts to half the sales tax-this case 3 per cent, with the exception of ties and that would be H per cent with the exception of piling which would be free. Does the minister catch the argument? It is a little involved, perhaps, but it is rather a vital matter.
Now the items which are free under the act are logs and round unmanufactured timber.
That is free by his-
That is free of the sales tax-

I am told by the customs that is the ruling they give in the department. I am just as anxious as my hon. friend not to discriminate against Canadian industry and if later on the point is established we will cure the difficulty. But I should not like to act without being sure of the ground I was on.
I point out to my hon. friend there is no distinction in principle whatever. I do not know what the department holds but there the fact is.
Let me come again to my point. The resolution as originally introduced was satisfactory. That is "'carbolic or heavy oil to be used in creosoting timber."

But it was not satisfactory to the customs. That is why the change was made. Under the act as originally introduced the case was ably presented by my hon. friend. I might be frank with him and say it was done to please him but I would not like him to think-

We appreciate it and the reason we are bringing the matter to the minister's attention, my colleague and I- and we are not criticising the minister-is to point out what the change really effects. I know the question is a complicated one and what we want to do is to try and get it settled correctly. When the minister introduced his first resolution it was perfectly satisfactory but the second resolution disturbs our minds very considerably.

I do not think my hon. friend needs to be disturbed. I am told by the customs it meets the case of my hon. friend. However I say to him now that if it does not we will make a correction; we have the power to do so.

I want to understand this clearly because I allowed the matter to go through last year and it worked a frightful hardship and meant tens of thousands of dollars of loss. I understood the first resolution to mean that creosote or carbolic or heavy oil which might be used in treating timber would be free of the sales tax. That has been altered and apparently only carbolic or heavy oil that goes into the creosoting of logs and round manufactured timber will be free of the sales tax. In other words if we use the carbolic oil in the production of anything else, such as railway ties, we will continue to pay 24 per cent on every gallon of creosote. My understanding is that if the creosote is to be purchased for anything
Ways and Means-Sales Tax

except creosoting logs and round manufactured timber it will have to pay the sales tax. That means that if a firm purchase this oil for any other purpose than creosoting logs and round unmanufactured timber, they will have to pay the tax. For instance, if they purchase the creosote for the purpose of creosoting railway ties, they must pay 2| per cent. Is that not correct?
Under the general act the creosote is exempt when used for anything that is going into an article that is liable to pay the tax.
Under the present amendment before the House, railway ties become subject to the tax for the first time.
They were liable to a tax of 6 per cent last year. It is now being reduced to 2| per cent.

That is the way it has been administered. There is no dispute about the 6 per cent. But the 6 per cent was never meant by the Finance Minister to apply, even under last year's amendment, to ereo-soted logs and round unmanufactured timber.
I am not committing myself in regard to last year.
If my hon. friend will ask his expert I think he will find that that was the assurance given by the Minister of Finance.

Anything going into any
material that is taxable is exempt.

That is where the difficulty apparently arose last year. These finished articles were not taxed, but it was assumed by the Minister of Finance and his experts that they were taxed. I am quite sure the intention of the Finance Minister last year- and I had his assurance and also the assurance of his expert in regard to it-that it was never intended that 6 per cent should apply, to the creosoted log and the round, unmanufactured timber. I would like to get that point clear if I can.
We are now endeavouring to correct any difference of opinion that existed last year, and we think we have corrected it.

It was not a difference of opinion; it was simply a difference of interpretation in the department over which the minister presides and the interpretation placed upon it by the Customs department. Is that correct?
I think that is right.
If it were simply a difference of opinion, as I suggest, I think it is only fair and reasonable that the minister should undertake to give a rebate of the sales tax in such cases.
I thought the hon. member was leading up to that.

I think the minister is
fair-minded enough to consider it only fair that I should lead up to that, and press upon the minister that he should consider the question of a rebate, because if it were never intended-and I pledge my word that it was never intended by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding)-that creosoting oil should be assessed 6 per cent, surely it is only fair and reasonable that a rebate should be given for the oil that has been purchased during the period that the 6 per cent tax was in effect, and the minister has power to grant the rebate. It has already been done in regard to some other articles this session. I think my hon. friend will agree that it is only reasonable and fair that, if the tax were never intended to apply, any tax that has been paid should be rebated, because otherwise, if my hon. friend does not grant this request, he becomes a party to giving a preference to the American manufacturers to the extent I have indicated. Undoubtedly this particular firm has lost a tremendous amount of business during the last year owing to the fact that the Americans have been shipping into our country their creosoted timber really under a bounty placed upon their goods by our own people. I am quite convinced that it was a bona fide mistake. All I ask is that the mistake be rectified and the rebate be given.

The hon. member who sits
directly in front of my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) knows that the minister who administers the Finance department never admits anything if he can avoid it; but I will promise my hon. friend that I will give consideration to the plea he has presented this afternoon, and when I have time I will look into the whole matter fully.

The minister
should look into the matter from this angle. Apparently we all agree that the Minister of Finance last year wanted to do what my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark) desires to have done this year; that he thought he was leaving the Canadian creosotor of ties in a position where he could do business and that so far as the Minister of Finance was concerned he carried out that intention, but that a different interpretation was placed upon the act, not by the gentleman who drew it, not

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
by the gentleman who knew what he wanted to bring about, but by the officers of the Customs department who had nothing whatever to do with its framing or its introduction into this House. I think we are agreed upon that. Then let us go a little bit further. If the minister agrees that that was the situation, a wrong was committed. The intention of the House and the intention of the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding), the active voice in the House in putting through that legislation, was never implemented. Furthermore there was practically an agreement and consent between all the parties but this agreement has been nullified. Members on this side of the House understood that the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) was doing what he said he was doing, and the Finance Minister understood that also. There is a mistake all round, and money has been paid under a mistake. Under such circumstances, in an ordinary court of law this money could be recovered, but conditions in courts of law do not apply here, of course. Surely the ordinary considerations which influence courts ought with far greater force apply to the government. In other words, in view of what is admitted here now, what possible moral defence would the government have if they hung on to this money and did not give the rebate? The minister appeals to me as former Minister of Finance. I would always strive, I always did strive when I had the honour of occupying the place that he now occupies, to do at least the honest thing, at least not to hold on to money that the country was not entitled to, to apply the provisions of the Audit Act in cases where refunds manifestly should be made, and I am sure that the minister will now tell the committee that the provisions of the act will be applied in this case and the refund made.

I shall have the matter very carefully looked into, and if it is established that there is a fair claim, it will be given fair consideration. I do not think the hon. member should ask me to go further than that. [DOT]

More than British Columbia is involved. Something in the Maritime provinces is also involved.

In the last two years and especially within the last year a great industry has been developed in the Maritime provinces in the manufacture of hardwood railway ties that are creosoted. Firms there have spent an enormous amount of money in establishing creosoting plants and equipment for sawing hardwood in mills that formerly sawed soft wood. One lumberman cut 6,000,000 feet of railway ties this year and he is creosoting them. I would like the minister to consider remitting the sales tax on the creosoted ties as well. I do not think the 2-J per cent will bring him any great amount of revenue, but it will mean a big
Ways and Means-Sales Tax

thing to those firms that are installing machinery and developing an industry only in its infancy in New Brunswick. Prior to the last two years hardwood was not, to my knowledge, manufactured into railway ties owing to the fact that such ties, when not creosoted, did not last very long, and this creosoting is practically a new thing. Our cedar, which we used for ties previously, is becoming depleted, and it is not as firm a wood as hardwood. Creosoting is becoming popular for railway ties, and I think if we consider the government's purchases of railway ties, it would be good business for the government to remit this tax on creosoted ties. When the Canadian Northern was built in New Brunswick, cedar ties were not available; spruce and tamarac were used, and I understand there w'ill be a replacement of ties in New Brunswick to a large extent. I should like the hon. member for Resti-gouche and Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) to urge the minister to consider this matter.

On account of the heavy engines used now on the Canadian National Railways, cedar ties are too soft, and after a short time the rail cuts the railway tie, especially the cedar one, putting the tie out of use altogether. In order to meet the situation, we have begun using creosoted hardwood ties. Within a very short time I am informed that a large business with a big plant is about to be developed at St. Leonard in my constituency. They have spent thousands and thousands of dollars in this new industry, and I hope the minister will take into consideration the prospects of this company which is establishing such a large industry at St. Leonard, and that he will take off all duties and sales tax on creosote oil, if at all possible. We are awaiting new development at the present time throughout Canada, and any action on the part of the government which will be of assistance in that connection will be greatly appreciated by the people at large. Those who are making ties in my constituency are especially farmers or settlers who are opening up new land. They prefer hardwood land to soft wood land because they claim that the soil is richer, and they have to dispose of that hardwood in some way. They have been selling the hardwood, at least the heavy stuff, for manufacturing, and I am sorry to say that hardwood, especially the large timber, is going across the boundary line, and free of duty too. We want to keep that industry at home if possible. We want to encourage
*Mr. Caldwell.]
in Canada the manufacture of ties as well as the manufacture of hardwood lumber in every line of industry.

My hon. friend has made a

The amendment is

Mr. Chairman, I am
probably in error, but just to show the difficulty of getting at this thing, I may say

that I started a while ago to look up some of these items. That accounts for it. It is all the more reason why we should have these things in extenso. I notice at the end of this resolution tariff items 86, 105 and 106. Item 86 is:
Tomatoes and other vegetables, including corn and baked beans, in cans or other airtight packages
Item 105 is:
Fruits in airtight cans, or other airtight packages.
And item 106 covers:

Two of these items are tinned and the third would be in glasses or tins. There is another article of food which is very important in the country from which I come. At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

What I was saying before recess was that fruits and vegetables in tins, generally speaking, are exempt from the sales tax. Representations have been made to me by Mr. Lewis Connors who has been the cause of considerable development in the fishing industry in New Brunswick, and who lately has acquired some properties on the west side of St. John harbour, where the actual canning of fish is being carried on. Generally speaking, sardines and some of the larger fish prove quite popular. That is an industry that is beneficial. It deals directly with the food of the people, just as much the food of the people as canned vegetables. I am not at all criticising the abolition of the sales tax on canned vegetables, but I fail to see any distinction between the canned vegetables and the canned fish. I am told also that the same question arises in British Columbia, where as we all know, salmon is canned in very large

Ways and Means-Sales Tar
quantities. I presume that there is some principle running through these changes, and I have gathered it to be in the direction of taking, so far as possible, the impost off the food of the people. Imported sardines may probably be classed among luxuries, but I think that the ordinary canned fish of this Dominion is not at all a luxury, and the further you get from the sea coast, the more it becomes an absolute necessity, if fish, which is a very valuable part of every man's diet, is to be had in decent condition. There are some parts where it is impossible to get fresh fish and fresh meat, and where canned fish is an excellent substitute for the ordinary diet.
I presume that this is not a matter of intention; I presume it is merely an oversight, and I trust that it is sufficient just to call the attention of the hon. minister to it to have the schedule amended so as to relieve, I would say, tinned or canned fish of all kinds from the impost.

I am quite anxious to
supplement what my hon. friend (Mr. Baxter) has said, and I would suggest to the minister that the figure 123, being tariff item 123, be inserted on the third line of page two of the ways and means resolutions, after the figure 106. Item 123 of Schedule A of the Tariff Act reads:
Salmon and all other fish prepared or preserved, including oysters-
And so on. That would include the canned fish to which reference has been made, and would cover canned salmon about which considerable has been said and correspondence had with the minister. That amendment, which I would ask the minister to accept, is very much along the line of the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Brandon on another score. It is simply enlarging slightly the exemptions, and is quite in harmony with the items set forth.

Representations have been
made to us from many sources asking for exemptions from the sales tax. Hon. gentlemen will admit that we must draw the line somewhere. The government must have the necessary revenue to carry on. It is quite true that we have added to the list of exemptions this year canned vegetables and certain canned fruits and jellies, but hon. members will observe that canned meats are not exempted, and, there is no good reason why canned fish should be placed in a different category from canned meats. I think it is a pretty fair tax on the boys who go out at night and buy lobsters and sardines; they should pay something towards the administration of the affairs of this country, and for
administration purposes, you cannot make exceptions of canned salmon and other fish. For these teasons I am unable to accept the amendment which has been urged by my hon. friends, much as I would like to meet their wishes. I think we will have to stop where we are this year.

Of course, the minister
settles the matter and we must accept his decision, but I would ask him why the sales tax is taken off these other things, jellies and fruits, as well as vegetables. I would ask him to state to the committee some principle which causes him to pick out one class of articles rather than another. I had supposed it was all on the basis of food, but apparently it is not. I would not have thought that fruits and jellies were as essential a part of the food of the ordinary Canadian citizen as fish. I may be wrong, but I would ask the minister to explain, so that we can undertsand just where we are.
For once I find myself-
I wonder if I will have an answer from the minister.

For once I find myself in full accord with my friends to my right. I think it is quite right to follow the principle of relieving the very necessaries of life from taxation as far as possible. I fully agree with them there.
I am very fortunate. I see the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) taking his seat. I wonder if he were to present this request to the minister, would it not receive better consideration?
He has done so already.

We are just presenting
to the minister-my colleague and I, supported by one or two others,-the request that canned salmon, item 123 in the tariff, should be added to the exempted, or at least to the reduced list. Canned salmon is included in the item of "canned fish". The item reads:
Salmon and other fish, prepared or preserved, ineluding oysters.	.
Now, up to the present my appeal and that of my colleague to the minister has not met with any response. I see the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) in his seat and as the minister has already responded twice very courteously and very kindly this afternoon to the suggestions of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) -after, I noticed, a little conference-and if
Ways and Means-Sales Tax

the hon. member for Skeena would support this appeal, which so far has been ineffective, it may be that the odium of granting anything to the Conservative party may be removed and the minister may grant the request to one of his own supporters. I do not care to whom he grants it, I think it is a fair request and it ought to be accepted. Canned fish, and particularly canned salmon, is a distinct item of food. It is a food in a far more important sense than the items we have here now, although I am not for a moment objecting to them. The minister has put items 105, 106 and 86 on the list. These relate to tomatoes and other vegetables. Then there is fruit in air-tight tins or other air-tight packages, and jelly, jams, preserves and condensed mince meats. Surely on the basis of making food cheaper for the public the addition of canned fish is a most reasonable request, and I am going to ask my hon. friend from Skeena to give me his support in this because I know very well that it meets with his approval and is a very important factor in the industries in his own riding.

I should have liked the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to have given me some notification of his intention so that I would have had an opportunity of discussing this matter. But as I have not had any chance to look into it I do not know just what is involved in the proposition. We propose closing a very expensive and extravagant central fisheries office at Vancouver and there may be necessity to meet expenditure by increasing the taxation on other commodities. However, I will be very glad indeed to discuss the reduction of the tax on canned salmon at some time soon.

My. hon. friend cannot
escape the issue by his promise to discuss the matter at. some future time. We are discussing the item right now. This is the time and the place for us to determine the issue. I am sorry that I have not got the support of the hon. member for Skeena but I shall proceed without it. Let me bring the matter again to the attention of the minister. Indeed I am going to move an amendment because I feel that I am warranted in doing so. The hon. gentlemen this afternoon moved amendments which immediately received the acceptance of the minister, and feeling confident in the precedent so established I will now move:
That the figures 123 be added after the figures 106 on the third line of page 2 of the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To whom is my
hon. friend referring?

Not to the Minister of
Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I asked the minister to lay down a line of demarcation so that we may know why some things are relieved from the tax .and others are not. Before the minister announces his decision I wish to endorse everything said by the hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). The fish canning industry is just in the infant stage on our stretch of the Atlantic coast. Not only is that industry putting up salmon in cans, but it is also canning lobsters, oysters, quahaugs, sardines and kippered herring. I submit all these are articles of food which should be considered on a par with canned vegetables, canned fruits, jams, jellies and condensed mincemeats. It will be observed that biscuits of all kinds are reduced to 2i per cent duty. I know hon. members will agree with me that biscuits do not to any extent appear on the tables of the poor, or for that matter on the table of the average family. Many lines of biscuits are virtually luxuries. Ice cream is placed on the free list but even that is not altogether as im-

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
portant to the poor man's table as canned salmon, canned kippered herring, and other varieties of fish when they cannot be obtained in their fresh state. Some few years ago the industry of shipping fresh fish from the Maritime provinces was in a thriving condition. To-day the market has somewhat declined, and during the season when the demand for fresh fish is small, different varieties can be canned and sold for food. I submit, Sir, that in keeping with the other modifications made today with respect to canned vegetables, fruits, jams and jellies, that canned fish should also be rated for duty at 2J per cent.

I suppose most of the committee realize that the policy of reducing the sales tax ought to be more or less gradual. We cannot	remove	the	sales tax	in	itsentirety at one stroke, and I agree with those who regard canned lobsters and canned oysters as luxuries. Only a very few people in this country can afford to buy such commodities, and as a matter of fact five-sixths of the lobsters canned in this country find a market either in the United States or Great Britain. That is an information I obtained from the Department of Trade and Commerce a few days ago.	Sardines	are	practically	in	thesame position. They are used to a greater extent in this country than lobsters or oysters. The oyster business in this country is not very important, but the lobster business is. I for one, although coming from a county where there are very many lobsters canned, perhaps as	many as	in	any county	in	theMaritime provinces,	do	not agree	at	this
stage, with the debt of the country such as it is, that the lobsters or the oysters should be relieved of the sales tax. As far as canned salmon is concerned, the minister says it is a matter of administration to leave it as it is at the present time. I agree with the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) that if the minister could regulate the present proposals without any great difficulty, perhaps he should take the matter of canned salmon into consideration. It is not in the same class as lobsters or oysters or some of the other fish mentioned. I would suggest to the minister that perhaps canned salmon should be relieved of the sales tax. if it were possible. These canned salmon are widely used in the . homes of the poor of the country and are not in the same category as oysters or lobsters.
Is it not a fact that there is no sales tax on canned lobsters exported?

No sales tax on any fish
exported.

Certainly 95 per cent-I would say 99 per cent-of canned lobsters are exported, and what is the trouble? Where is the difficulty and injustice? There is a large percentage of canned salmon consumed in Ontario, I daresay; but I presume nothing at all compared with the quantity exported, upon which there is no sales tax. I was a little surprised to see my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. Doucet) so anxious to reduce the cost of food to the poor people and remove the taxation. That is a very commendable thing, but a few days ago he moved an amendment to the budget to increase the taxation on everything. That is not a logical position nor is it consistent, but I am glad to see my esteemed friend improving and recognizing the fact that the people are desirous of reducing the cost of everything, particularly the cost of food, the cost of the necessaries of life and the cost of implements of production. I am sure he now regrets that he moved the amendment, and that he will sin no more in that respect.

The amendment which was discussed a few days ago is not before the House this evening. If it were I might enlighten my hon. friend from Kings, P. E.I., (Mr. Hughes). If 95 per cent of our lobsters are being exported-and	it is
admitted that 95 per cent are being exported -we need not worry about the class of people in this country who use the other 5 per cent. We are not worrying on their behalf, but we contend that the poor class of our population who have to buy canned salmon and canned fish of other kinds, such as canned oysters, clams, quahaugs, sardines and kippered herrings, which are industries of some importance in this Dominion, should not be held down by the fact that the product is placed in a very unenviable position as far as the necessaries of life are concerned. They all make part and parcel of the dinner-table of the poor man. My hon. friend from Kings, P.E.I. has evidently forgotten that a few days ago he spoke on behalf of the poor people of the country, and possibly I learned a lesson from him. But I submit the poor classes of the Dominion are anxious to have the sales tax removed as much as possible from the necessaries of life. I contend that the cutting off of the sales tax on canned fish is a step in the right direction.

Coming from the Pacific
coast where the canned salmon industry is a very important one, I may say that this is becoming an article of food all over the
Ways and Means-Sales Tax

country, even miles away from the coast. It is one of our most important industries, and is a general article of food everywhere. I think the minister should seriously consider the removal of the tax on this food. Salmon canners, on the other hand have not had the good times that prevailed before the war, when the runs of salmon were very much larger than they are at the present time. They are working under difficulties that did not prevail before, both with regard to high wages and other matters and greater cost of production, and the removal of the sales tax would certainly be a great boon, not only to the salmon producers, but also to the salmon consumers throughout Canada. Therefore. I wish to endorse what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and other hon. members who supported him have to say in this House.

If it were only a question
of canned salmon, it might be very easy, but a question of administration enters into the amendment presented by my hon. friend, which includes canned salmon, canned lobsters and canned sardines, and I submit again that is a fair source of taxation. We made considerable reductions in the sales tax this year. If we accepted the amendment now, there would be no good reason why we should not immediately have another resolution introduced that we should exempt canned meats, and that would involve under the classification canned soups, of which there is a million and a half imported into this country. speechtext:
Then an amendment
has been moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens).

I desire to say a few words in support of this amendment, particularly with regard to salmon canned in the province of British Columbia. No industry in this country has been more depressed than the salmon canning industry, and I do not think there is any industry more deserving of consideration at this moment. The government has seen fit to reduce and, in fact, to eliminate the sales tax as regards many items. It has seen fit to reduce the sales tax, I think, to 2j per cent on all canned goods with the exception of canned meats. There is a great distinction between canned meat and canned salmon. In British Columbia canned salmon is a very important item, and it is an important item in the diet of the people of Canada generally, much more so than canned meat. In the case of meat, the producer of beef, for instance, has his herds; he can control the herds; he always knows what he has. But the case of fish is quite different; each year the salmon canner goes out and catches all the fish he can, and his catch is a matter of speculation. Then he must can them. In view of the fact that this industry is in a state of depression and needs encouragement and assistance, and in view of the fact that the government has seen fit to give encouragement to the canning of fruits and vegetables, it is only consistent that the same consideration should be extended to the salmon canning industry.

I look on the matter in a somewhat different light. A man builds a cannery; he catches fish and he cans them. He does not have to feed or care for them before he catches them. A man raising cattle has to feed and look after the cattle for three or four years before he can sell them or can them. I am not finding fault with the salmon canners. That industry is of great importance to British Columbia. But if we are going to take this tax off one thing after another, where are the finances of the country going to come from? I think the people ought to appreciate what the government has done in regard to lowering taxes. It has lowered the sales tax. I was rather surprised this afternoon to hear that so many people had not paid

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
their sales taxes for two or three years. I am interested in a business and I know we have to pay our sales tax the fifteenth of the following month. If we do not do so, we hear from the department. If there is going to be a reduction in the sales tax as regards foods, it certainly ought to be in connection with canned meats and other things along that line.

I understand the amendment refers to taking the tax off canned salmon, canned lobster, canned oysters and canned sardines. I agree somewhat with the view of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that lobsters and oysters are more or less luxuries. People who indulge in oyster or lobster suppers at midnight can afford to pay the sales tax. The situation as regards canned salmon is different. It is the poor man's diet. I would suggest that a compromise might be arranged, and if anyone will support me, I beg to move as an amendment to the amendment:
Provided that the reduction shall apply only to canned salmon.
So that the sales tax will be taken off salmon, but left upon oysters, lobsters and sardines.

I shall be pleased to
second the motion. I fully agree that as 95 per cent of the lobsters are exported, the matter is not very important whether the sales tax is taken off or not. Oysters, I will submit, are more or less of a luxury. One of the reasons why I did not speak before was because I was before the minister some time ago with a delegation endeavouring to persuade him to take the sales tax off sardines.

The amendment to the
amendment does not include sardines.

I should like to ask
the mover of the amendment to the amendment if it includes salmon and sardines.

That the words, " canned salmon and canned small herring " *be added after the word " smoked " in line fifteen of the said resolution.
The effect will be to include in the exemption list canned salmon and canned herring. A similar argument on behalf of this food will, I think, apply to northern Ontario, portions of Quebec, and the eastern provinces. Mr. Chairman, we have already voted on the issue of canned salmon, and I am not sure that the amendment of my hon. friend is in order.

But quite apart from the point of order, I must point out that the resolution is impossible; it cannot be administered by the department.

I should certainly like
the minister to enlighten us on his objection. How can it be more difficult to administer the Special War Revenue Tax Act in regard to leaving canned salmon or canned pilchards off than it is in exempting canned fruits and canned jellies? What is the difference in administration? Does it take a more skilful inspector 
to discover whether the fish contained in a can are salmon or pilchards than to detect whether the contents of another can are jelly or jam? There surely is nothing in such an objection. I do not wish to appear impertinent to the minister, but frankly I cannot see any possible excuse for the objection from the administrative standpoint.
Let me add this. This is a very simple item. Let us take canned salmon, for instance, first. On the Pacific coast, which I think is really the chief location of the industry, the canneries can salmon and very little else. They export a certain amount. The government have to take cognizance of the export and exempt that from the tax. Now we are simply asking them to exempt it all. A large portion of the pack is exempt already- I suppose 75 per cent. The department must keep track of that 75 per cent and distinguish between it and the other 25 per cent sold in this country. We are proposing to relieve the department of that function; they do not have to take cognizance of any if it is all exempt.
Let us come now to the pilchards. At the present time we ship a large quantity, I suppose from 50 to 75 per cent of our pack, to Australia, Japan, South America, and other trans-Pacific points; some goes to the Old Country and the West Indies. All of that is exempt. The department must carefully distinguish between what is exported and what is sold at home, and I am asking that the minister shall be relieved of that function. There is no added administration there; indeed, there is a simplification of administration, unless I am wholly ignorant of what administration means and what its functions are.

My hon. friend, living on the
coast, is I am sure better posted on fish than I am. Will he tell me the difference between small herring and sardines?

Yes, I will tell him the
difference. I will venture to say, so far as the Pacific coast is concerned, and that is all I undertake to speak for, that there are no real sardines on the Pacific coast. I am told the same is true of the Atlantic coast, although I am not speaking for the Atlantic coast; but I do know that these smaller herring are put up into cans as sardines and sold as sardines very often. Any of the fishery officers are quite qualified to determine the character of the fish, and I am sure they will advise the minister to that effect. My hon. friend smiles, I do not know just why.

I was not smiling; I am very serious.

I was referring to the
minister. Perhaps he is smiling at the thought of being advised by those sitting behind him.

For the minister to say for one moment that it is more difficult to administer the exemption from the sales tax in the case of canned herring or canned salmon than in the case of canned fruits of various kinds-well, it is beyond me. Mr. Chairman, I desire to move the amendment which I have already placed in your hands. In connection with this amendment I have a carefully prepared speech supporting it. I am referring to lumber, and the speech reads:
Take the tax on lumber and on material that goes into the construction of a house or barn. I am told by a responsible contractor that on a $5,000 house, which is not an extravagant average price, the materials going into that house represent $3,500. The minister proposes to put a tax of $105 against that house; there is no question about that. The minister puts a tax of $105 against the building of a house at a time when every one is calling for more houses in this country. The same is true with regard to the building of barns throughout the country. I am told by the same contractor that the average cost of the material going into a modern barn would be 80 per cent of a $2,000 building. The minister proposes to put a tax on that $1,600 worth of materials of $48. He is hampering production to that extent.
Mr. Chairman, those are the sentiments of an hon. member of this House. At that time he was the hon. member for Valleyfield; today he is the hon. Acting Minister of Finance. Those were his sentiments when we had a sales tax a fraction of the sales tax we have to-day, and I am perfectly convinced that all I have got to do is to point out the situation to the minister and he will very gladly accept the amendment. What does the amendment do, after all? Why, it does just exactly what the hon. member urged very strongly when the tax was, as I say, very much smaller than it is to-day. He was 161
wanting to help, then. I am going to ask him whether he would not be helping a great deal more in doing what he thought should be done in 1921, than in putting fancy foods on the free list, fancy biscuits, ice cream, and the like. I suppose there is no room for question as to that, not even by my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes). I have heard him-yes, and I have heard gentlemen to my left-talk time and again about the iniquity of getting a tax back at the origin, that the nearer down you have it to the consumer the less it costs the consumer. Well, we had a calculation made last year and we took that added tax, that 6 per cent tax as against the 4i per cent tax, and we applied the ordinary profits coming down from the manufacturer, the wholesaler and the retailer to the consumer and we ascertained that the public had to pay Ilf per cent in order that the government might get the 6 per cent my hon. successor was legislating for. There is no doubt whatever as to the effect of the law. It never was challenged, it was not even challenged in the debate.
What does my hon. friend say the average was under the 50 per cent increase ?

Under our 50
per cent increase-there rvas no secret about it-the traders came here and sought to have a change made. down to New York the week after my hon. friend's budget first came in with a large wholesaler, who stated that they were at last getting fairness. I said, "What did I do to you?" The point I want to make is that as regards the imposition of a sales tax, which is placed upon many transactions, the weight upon the taxpayers of the country will depend upon the number of transactions upon which the sales tax is placed and upon the rate of profit that the different merchants and manufacturers will add to the sales tax as they collect it. That is perfectly plain. The tax pyramids. In the case under consideration, where I do not think my right hon. friend will object either to the number of transactions or to the rate of profit, the sales taxes which applied under the former regime aggregated $19.73, and on those the profits that were collected amounted to $12.82, making the total sales tax amount to over 30 per cent. I say that in cases like that the burden on the consumer was heavier than under the present regime.
The object that hon. gentlemen in the coiner opposite have in proposing resolutions of this sort is easy to be seen. For a number of years they had the control of the treasury in their hands. They had the power of reducing sales taxes on lumber and such things as that. They did not reduce the tax. They propose now to reduce a sales tax to a level which their sales taxes had; but it seems to me that we have to consider this in the House:	The government are responsible,

Their plans provided for substantial reductions in the sales tax. on that thing, and appealing to the low-tariff and non-taxing sentiment of the country. But it is hardly fair and it is hardly consistent coming from a party which prides itself upon being a high-tariff and protectionist party of this country.

Rudeness, which is very unusual coming from my right hon. friend to me, is not argument.

This motion is what? To put this tax where we had it, where we endorsed it, where we supported it and where we left it, in which position we. resisted the attacks of the hon. member himself to make it still less, resisted the attacks of the present Minister of Finance who severely criticised us for imposing this tax on the building of a home or a barn and whose words were re-echoed with wonderful eloquence by the hon. member for Brome. I do not want to be misrepresented.

I do not want to misrepresent my hon. friend.
I accept that. I said that in a series of sales such as the one exposed in my example, the aggregate of the sales taxes amounted to some 19.73 per cent.

Does the hon. gentleman imagine that any man is worth while quoting who would suggest that in any case 19 per cent or in any case 30 per cent was added to the cost to the consumer? The thing is so monstrous that it does not appeal to the mind of the hon. member. I know it does not. I know he would not look me in the face in private conversation and say so. The thing is utterly ridiculous; it is monstrous; it is a joke-30 per cent to the consumer on a one and one-half and one and one-half per cent tax, and! the cost of living, all the while the tax was on, reduced 28 points according to the official records of this government! How could such a thing occur? The taxes were never imposed at those points at all, and not a member of' this ministry, that has collected them on the same system, with the tax increased 50 per cent at each point, will stand up to-night and say that in one instance was it ever collected at the points cited by the hon. member for Brome. I know they will not. I defy them to do so now. If it was and if that applied!, under that we collected 373,656,489. Under the system of this government, which included, I know, only three months of the latest imposition-but the three months were equal in the average revenue to the nine months that went before -and that answers the hon. member-they collected $120,574,000 with business declining all over this country, as is evidenced by the collections of income tax and by every other return.
I do not think that is a true evidence, because you might have as large a business, run it on a lower percentage of profit and have a smaller income tax.

That is amusing too.
Imagine accounting for a falling off of income tax collections by such reasoning as that. Even conceding that,-and I do not concede it, but I will let the hon. member dlo that if he likes-that there was a somewhat greater business in 1923 than in the year that ended the 31st March, 1921, there was very much better business in the year 1921 than there was in 1924, as every hon. member who is in business knows. But conceding a fractional increase, how does the hon. member account 
for the difference between 373,000,000 and $120,000,000? Does he suggest that he can account for it? He can account for it only by the higher imposition of the sales tax, and he knows it. I will not follow his lead in trying to introduce the subject of protection into a sales tax issue; they are as distinct as any two classes of taxes that ever existed. When we come to protection we will discuss it, and all we hope and pray is that the hon. gentleman and all his friends will stand by their guns when that issue comes to be decided.

speechtext:
There are
three collections in that transaction.

Now, what I want to point out to the House is this. The argument is constantly used that when these goods are sold .the full cost is charged with the addition.of the duty. This point has been brought up in the House so frequently that I think it would pay hon. members to study the schedules. They are too intricate to go into in detail at the moment, but they will appear in Hansard and are very enlightening. Manufacturers generally, as well as wholesalers and other business men, do not fix their price in that way at all. Rather they take the cost of production, and this cost, whether it is of the goods in the hands of the manufacturer or in the hands of the wholesaler, is primarily the cost of the raw material, secondly the freight and carriage, and then if there is a duty it is added as a part of the cost of the goods. It makes no difference whether it is the sales tax or any other kind of tax, it is added. If there is insurance, if there is rent, if there are taxes on the building, all these things, or a great many of them, naturally enter into the overhead charges of the business, and only such charges enter into the cost of ithe goods as directly affect the goods themselves. It does not follow that because the duty is 10, 20 or 30 per cent the price of the goods manufactured is increased by that percentage, nor is that duty pyramided along the whole line of these transactions. But certainly wherever a tax is imposed, whether it be income tax, sales tax, stamp tax, real estate tax or a rental,-any and all of these enter into the general overhead cost of the business; there is no question of that.- And there is no question at this point that the

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
aggregate of these taxes and charges, insurance and so forth, is entered as part of the cost of the goods so produced. In 1922 a duty was imposed on imported clothing, and the wholesaler importing such goods paid the duty of 30 per cent, we will say-I have forgotten the exact duty; it was 30 or 35 per cent-and $100 worth of the goods when they reached the wholesalers' warehouse represented a cost of $130. But there was a general fall of prices all over the country, and in nearly every case in the clothing business the slump was such that the wholesale price to the retail dealer was actually below the cost of the goods plus the duty paid by the wholesaler, and the goods were sold to the retailer 10 p.m. and passed on to the public at a figure less than their cost plus duty. In that case the wholesaler assisted in the paying of the duty; he paid more duty than the consumer paid. Does my hon. friend get that point?
Yes.

If that is the case, and
undoubtedly it is, why was it charged by Mr. Pedlow in his memorandum that this duty is always pyramided and passed on to the consumer? I will admit that such a condition does not always obtain; but the point we ought to keep in mind is that the dealer in goods has to absorb the loss on a falling market, just as he receives sometimes the advantage on a rising market. What I want to complain of, if I may, is that attitude of mind which invariably attaches to the business men of Canada some sort of an offence against the public because the duty is made a part of his cost. But let me repeat this: The duty is no more a part of his cost than his real estate taxes.
Just as much a part of it.

Just as much a part of it. It is a tax on his business and is a part of his cost. A man, for instance, pays taxes on his factory, pays insurance on his factory, pays interest on the money he borrows to handle his business, what we call working capital-ail these things go into the general cost of his business; they all play a part in the cost of production, and when the article is finished it represents the cost of material, plus rent or taxes as the case may be, insurance, interest on capital, interest on working capital or bank overdraughts, as the case may be. These all form a part of his cost, and the cost price of that article is then fixed.
I do not wish to pursue the point any further, but I did think my hon. friend might
have given to the committee this memorandum as well. Furthermore, he will recall that this thing was submitted to an economist, unless my memory plays me false, and I do not think it does; it was submitted, if I remember rightly, to Dr. Adam Shortt, a gentleman for whom I have the highest regard, and there was a conference between the chairman, Dr. Adam Shortt, and Mr. Sparks, and, I believe, Mr. Pedlow, although I am not sure of that. I see the hon. member nods his head; Mr. Pedlow was there also. But why did not my hon. friend call Dr. Adam Shortt before the committee, and let the committee of his fellow-members have the benefit of consultation with Dr. Shortt? I recall, if I am not mistaken again, that while at first Dr. Adam Shortt subscribed to the doctrine that Mr. Pedlow advanced, after a study of these schedules presented by Mr. Sparks he agreed that they were just as sound or more sound than the schedules presented by Mr. Pedlow, and the criticism I would offer of my hon. friend's action is not only his presenting it in the way he did to-night, but in failing last year to give the agricultural committee the privilege and the opportunity of following this intricate question to an ultimate conclusion, and it could only be done before such a committee with ample time for study.
