speechtext:
My hon.
friend has just cited a case himself, and my hon. friend from Brome cited a case of the same character. It possibly would not apply to the item under discussion, that of lumber, but taking the whole field of sales generally in Canada, it does apply.

I will not detain the
committee long in reply to my hon. friend. I first, however, wish to make this point perfectly clear, that there was no difference between Mr. Sparks and Mr. Pedlow on the question .as to what the sales tax amounted to. Just as the hon. member who has taken his seat has disclosed to the House, I read from the proceedings of the special committee, part 1, page 910 from the exhibit quoted by my hon. friend:
First sales tax, 3f per cent on invoice price plus duty $5.06; second sales tax, manufacturer to wholesaler, $3.93; third sales tax, $10.74.
Now if you add those three sales taxes together, according to Mr. Sparks, you find that the sales tax aggregated $19.73 on this $100 bill of goods, so there is no difference between Mr. Pedlow and Mr. Sparks as far as the aggregate amount of these three sales taxes in this example are concerned. Where they did differ, and I am perfectly frank to say there was a difference of opinion, was that Mr. Pedlow said that when importers paid duty and sales tax they regarded that as constituting the price of their goods, and they made a percentage of advance, not upon the invoice price, but upon the full amount the goods cost laid down in their warehouse; that when the wholesaler sold to the retailer, that is the same amount on which he calculated his profit, and when the retailer sold again to the consumer, he calculated his profit, not upon any percentage of his overhead, but knowing what the goods cost him, he added a certain percentage. That was the theory of Mr. Pedlow, and I think it is the theory which every merchant in this country follows. Mr. Sparks had a somewhat complicated and refined way of putting on only a certain part of the advance that Mr. Pedlow put on. He made long and intricate calculations of overhead, but I believe Mr. Ped-low's was the simple and the more usual way of conducting business and of calculating prices, and I think most merchants in this House will agree with him. But my remarks are characterized as this tissue of absurdities

-no that is not the exact word-this knot of absurdities,-and the leader of the opposition took that from Macaulay's essay on Southey's Soliloquies on Society; it is interesting to know just where he got these somewhat, I hope, badly applied words which he used to pour ridicule on my devoted head-because I had said the three sales taxes aggregated $19.73. Then one of his seconds-in-command, or thirds-in-command, or fourths-in-command, got up in the House and praised Mr. Sparks to the highest, and then made out from Mr. Sparks' own statement that he calculated the aggregate sales tax exactly at the same figure Mr. Pedlow reached. The difference between the two was this. Mr. Pedlow estimated that the sales tax plus profit on sales tax amounted to $32 and some odd cents; Mr. Sparks calculated that the sales tax, and profits on sales tax, amounted to $24.41. In one case Mr. Sparks thought that the pyramiding of the sales tax amounted to $4.63. Mr. Pedlow put it at a very much higher figure. But the point I want to make is this and after all these differences of opinion between merchants are a secondary matter: That both these men- who are honest and who are intelligent-came before the committee and they both agreed that the sales tax in this case was 19.73 per cent; they both admitted they pyramided the tax and took considerably more out of the consumer than the treasury received.

I do not know that we will ever get to a common ground in connection with this matter, but there are some things that are absolutely common to everybody and we know of them. For example, we know where the 6 per cent came from, we know the gentleman who prepared it, we know his pamphlet which was adopted, and we know that the whole scheme was a scheme of the manufacturer in one particular line of business. We also know what the trade papers say, and I am very much more interested in what the general trade papers say than in what is said by an isolated merchant here or an isolated merchant there. My hon. friend from Brome himself would not think for a moment that was a fair example of the manner in which business was done in Canada. He could not because he knows that if he did all the government figures are simply absurd. Now I take the trade papers. I take a reference which I find at page 2705 of last year's Hansard. Hamilton is a great place for jobbers, and this is what I find at the page mentioned:
Hamilton, Ont., May 12.-Jobbers are particularly pleased with the budget especially in its treatment of the sales tax.

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
" It's a good budget for the jobbers," stated St. Clair Balfour, of Balfour Smye Limited, wholesale grocer.
" It gives us just what we have been after for a long time. Hitherto with a one per cent tax we had to absorb the sales tax."
" We could not avoid it. Now, however, this tax will be placed on at the point of manufacture and we will be relieved of this trouble."
Asked if this would not result in pyramiding Mr. Balfour readily admitted it would be the case.
" Oh, yes, certainly " he said, " If the article costs $100 and the manufacturer puts on the $6 sales tax, we will collect our profit on the $106."
The real truth is that merchants and manufacturers found they could not pass it on altogether, and in many cases not at all. They do pass this on now and you see it in connection with the cost of living expenses. But all this is by the way. There was one particular line of business, it was pointed out, would mean more than two transactions as a rule. That line of business was lumber, in the way that lumber is handled and, the number of people whose hands it passes through, it was shown, and particularly on the prairies, that there were often more than two transactions in lumber; and, of course, it would be said then that therefore our taxation was much higher. That is the argument at once. But in order to prevent that, our law provided that in respect of lumber an excise tax of 3 per cent should be imposed, levied and collected on sales and deliveries by the Canadian manufacturer, and that further excise taxes would not be payable on resales. So that apart from all argument we have to-day got five per cent on lumber as against three per cent under the old law. Now, I ask my hon. friend if he was wrong in 1921? Wore his figures incorrect? Were the principles he was advocating incorrect?
I ask him that plain and simple question?

My hon. friend has quoted
against me this evening the speech I made in 1921 when we were imposing new taxes upon the people. He appears to have forgotten, however, that in introducing the budget we remitted some 824,000,000 of taxes that had been imposed, we remitted all the taxes upon agricultural implements, and this afternoon we have made some further concessions in the shape of remission of taxes on certain appliances used on the farm and in the fisheries. I want to say frankly to my hon. friend that while I am not at all out of sympathy with 'his idea as it will apply to rough lumber only, it is my duty to provide revenue and to see that we have sufficient revenue to carry on the business of the country for the year. Under these conditions I would ask my hon. friend not to press his amendment. I am told by lumbermen-lumbermen of experience-that they like the present rates better than the rates that prevailed prior to January 1. As the tax applied before it was three per cent on the rough lumber but when it was worked up into doors, sashes, panelling, and all other things used in the construction of a house, the cost was added so that in the end it cost very much more. All things considered I think my hon. friend would be very well advised if he would not press his amendment. It is true that I did make suggestions to Sir Thomas White at that time but I did not go so far as to offer an amendment to his resolution.

I feel that some figures have been given to the House to-night that should not go unchallenged. I am not so much concerned as to the basis upon which they are made-whether upon statements made by Mr. Sparks before the agricultural committee or by Mr. Pedlow. Naturally as I was a member of that committee I am somewhat interested. I presume both gentlemen were honest and that both of them gave what they believed to be correct figures. I assume also that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) was honest in quoting these figures or using this illustration. However, to my mind the statement is not perfectly clear based upon the illustration that he uses. He stated that because there was pyramiding, and in one case the sales tax was paid about three times, the amount actually paid into the treasury on $100 of the first investment was $19.73, being practically 19.73 per cent. I believe I am correct in this statement. That was the amount he says actually paid into the treasury. Now he says, under the present system there is only 6 per cent collected at the source and only $6 is actually paid into the treasury. Unless the hon. member for Brome can explain the situation satisfactorily the remainder of his argument must naturally fall to the ground because when 19.73 per cent was actually paid into the treasury the total amount of the collection was $72,000,000, but when it was reduced to 6 per cent and $6 actually paid in, the total receipts were about $120,000,000. These figures are so much at variance, so completely ridiculous, that the hon. member will have difficulty in extricating himself from an awkward position, and his well meant advice so frequently directed to this comer of the chamber must continue to fall on deaf ears.

I do not intend to proceed with the argument further, but I understand the hon. member (Mr. McMaster) has sought to rob me of the originality of the
Ways and Means-Sales Tax

expression to which I took exception. I cannot submit to that even though it is attributed to a name very much revered. I only ask, now that he finds that someone else whom I know he admires used the expression, he will no longer think it rude.
I accept the statement so graciously made by my right hon. friend.

I should have been out of the House some time ago to fulfil another engagement, but if I left the House before a vote was taken I know what remarks would be made by some of my hon. friends to the right; so I will stay until the vote is taken.
I happen to remember some of the choice phrases which I heard the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) use, and I am going to give the House one or two of them, just to show what a tremendous vocabulary he can employ at times. These expressions are as follows: Shameless duplicity; Sickly affectation; Blazing madness. These are a few of the phrases. I rather admire them. They are quite forcible and count for something in debate. They are all right. I am not finding any fault with them. I must say I enjoy the speeches of the right hon. member. They are generally very telling, and forcibly delivered.
In regard to the question before the committee, it seems to me it is, simply: Should there be a sales tax on lumber? That appeals to members in this part of the House immediately-to reduce taxation if possible on any materials that may be of ordinary use on the farm and elsewhere. But there have been material reductions made. I realize that we require a revenue. I had considerable concessions made to me with regard to certain articles used on the farm. On the other hand, I am pretty sure that the amount of lumber that will be used upon the farm during the coming summer will not be very great, and it will not make very much difference to the average agriculturist what the price of lumber is during the next summer.
Is the hon. member thinking of the farm only?

I am speaking of the farm only-exactly what I am speaking of. Lumber may be used in other directions, but I know very well that the trouble has been handed over to this part of the Hoflse because it will affect the farmer. The sales tax is not one that we like to pay. We realize that it is burdensome, and would like to see it abolished altogether but I feel, under the circumstances, that I cannot support the amendment at the present time. I know very well the purpose to which all these votes will be 
put. I have no hesitation in endorsing what the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has said but I have no intention of being made a catspaw to pull the chestnuts out of the fire for any person in this House. I will be judged on my record just exactly the same as other hon. members, and I am not at all afraid. I think I can form an opinion myself and act accordingly, and no member will have the ability to drive me from what I think to be the right course.
Did my hon. friend make his proposals to embarrass? If he did not why should he ascribe any such motive to members on this side of the House?
Members on that side of the House rarely rise that they do not turn to hon. members to their left.
Let the leader of that great party answer my question.
What is your question?
Did you make your proposals to embarrass?
Order, order.

Did the hon. leader of the Progressive party make his proposals to embarrass the government, or from the standpoint of necessity and of need? If he made the proposals for the latter reason, why should he ascribe other motives to any other hon. member of the House?

For the simple reason that
nearly every hon. member who rises in that corner of the House turns to members to his left. It is a favorite trait.
We like to look at you.
That is all very well. If such is not the fact, do not get annoyed.
I am not annoyed.

In the opinion of the hon. leader of the Progressive party, is it better to have exemption from sales tax on fancy goods than on lumber? I will give the hon. member another question. Does he think ice cream is more important than lumber?
Mr. Chairman-
I have asked the hon. member for Brandon a question, and the hon. member need not answer.

The minister will not
answer questions addressed to himself; why should he answer questions put to the Progressive leader?

we have received from the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), I am sure hon. members are not at all surprised that some of us who have sat here silent for some time should have something to say. We have become accustomed to receiving advice and lectures of this kind from the leadter of the group to our left. It appears that he is quite satisfied that he has been driving a bargain with the hon. members who represent the government, or the government themselves, and he says "Because they have granted my demands along certain lines, I think it is up to me now to concede something in return." This is the kind of bargaining to which we have been subjected during the whole session. This is something that was in effect even before the House met; and yet we are supposed to remain in our seats and take a lecture from the hon. member for Brandon. It is a bargain and sale-nothing short of it- and it has been going on all during the session. The hon. member for Brandon now rises in his place and says, "This would be a very nice thing for the farmer, but the farmer has already received a great deal in the way of concessions at the hands of the government." What about the people living in the towns and cities who have to buy building material for their houses? We were granting loans to the poor people to enable them to build houses. The hon. member has no sympathy with those people when considering the tax that is now being imposed upon them. I would not have spoken on this matter had it not been for the remarks which the hon. member has just made. Rest assured that if the government finds itself in an indefensible position we will find the hon. member for Brandon attempting to defend them, and, judging from the defence he puts up, I do not think the government are very grateful to him sometimes for his attempt to come to the rescue.

I am sure I accept the
reprimand I have received in a very grateful spirit. This afternoon I moved an amendment which was carried by a majority in this chamber, and the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) said that I was bargaining with the government. I do not see what bargaining there is when you move an amendment and it is carried.

When was that amendment
voted on?

The hon. member was
out of the chamber.

I am going to ask the Chairman if there was a vote in this House to-day on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Brandon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It was declared carried.
No vote and no discussion. What happened was that my hon. friend went over, discussed it with the minister, got his consent, and it was declared carried.

All we find fault with is that the hon. member does not go over there and stay there. Let him stand out true before this country exactly what he is, a bargainer with the government, a bargainer day by day, an accessory to the government and all its works. That is what he is. Let him go and merge with thern^ and present a straight front before the people of Canada. Then we have something we can understand. But this procedure of playing at one end, and sticking by a group party in the West, to pretend to be urging for one policy when his party is really supporting the government in another policy, is what we object to. That is not straight politics. Instead of looking across the aisle, with his eye meeting that of the leader of the government in a confession of mutual virtue, and claiming that there is no bargain when the bargain is written across the face of everything done in this House, let him go over as a straight supporter of the government and take all he can with him. Let us have two parties and fight the issue in this country, and let the will of the majority rule.

I have just one remark to
make and then I am through. I think the language used by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is not language that is fitting coming from the leader of a great party in this House to myself.

My hon. friend referred
to resolutions moved-I moved two of them this afternoon and my colleague, whom I joined, moved the third-as motions deliberately designed to obstruct and to embarrass and moved for no other reason. That statement is absolutely without the slightest foundation in fact. I moved two resolutions genuinely designed and based upon one idea, namely, to give effect to what the government says, to reduce the tax upon food. What were those two resolutions? The first was

I do not recollect-

I saw him. My hon.
friend's recollection is very faulty. He rose in his place and he said to the minister that he thought it was a very good move and resolution, with the exception that it included oysters and lobsters. The resolution was before the Chair. We voted on it and it was voted down. Then, in order to meet the objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Forke), I moved a second resolution, exactly what he asked for, and again the resolution was voted down. Now, he comes along and gives this comer of the House a lecture upon how to present resolutions. He impugned our motives. He is constantly impugning our motives, simply because we have principles, ideas and convictions whfth we are not afraid to stand by in this House. My hon. friend stands in his place and, with a great deal of sanctity in his expression and tone, in a tone of superiority, of self-righteousness, the tone that the Pharisees used-
Oh, oh.

Let my hon. friends say "oh, oh," if they like. We have been sitting here long enough listening to these lengthy lectures from the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke). Not a move is made by hon. members in this section of the House but its motives are impugned.. He also moved one or two resolutions; but my hon. friend (Mr. Forke) pussy-footed across the chamber, whispered for a few minutes in the ear of the minister, came back and moved two resolutions regarding two items which I have before me. These two items were windmills which he wanted on the free list and portable engines. What was the little by-play? Why, a child couldl see through it. After tripping across the floor of the House and whispering for about five minutes in the ear of the minister, he came back again and, with an air of innocence and sanctity, he moved his resolution. The minister, completing the childish by-play, got up and said. "Yes, I think we will accept it; it is a perfectly proper resolution." Why, it is part of the price the government is paying for support: It is part of the blood money of the politics of this country. That is what it is.
Oh, oh.

It is part of the price being paid for the votes of hon. gentlemen in this 
House to pull this government through, and nothing else, and it would not be considered for five minutes by the government if the government had a majority behind them. Then, my hon. friend not only stands in his place, but goes out before the public constantly making insinuations as regards the morals, intentions and motives of hon. gentlemen in this section of the House. We are just a little bit sick of this and we do not purpose standing it very much longer. I reiterate- and I stand behind what my leader has said-let hon. gentlemen to my left, under the leadership of the hon. member for Brandon, who has given and who is giving slavish support to this government, join the government forces honourably and manfully, and stand behind them. Then, at least, we shall , have respect for them. We have respect for hon. gentlemen wherever they sit when they bring forward their opinions of policy upon which they are prepared to stand and fall but as regards this seesawing and pussyfooting, going across the floor and saying to the minister "Now, if you will accept this, I will move it, but if you do not want to accept it, I will rot move it. Will it embarrass you? If it does not embarrass you, I will move it." Or, "Mr. Minister, let me move this. You see you did not bring this down in the budget; but if you let me move this item, it will help me with my farmer friends in the West and I shall be able to go back West and say: ' Look at what I have done; I have got windmills on the free list'- this pussy-footing and bargaining does not become the hon. gentleman very well. In fact, he has no particular qualifications which warrant him in standing, not monthly, but daily in hie place and reading little curtain lectures to us for our actions in this House. These actions that we are taking, the part that we are taking, the position that we take on the tariff, we take fairly; we do not take it simply because it is helping us here or there, but because it is our policy. We believe in protection; we believe in a consistent, intelligible principle of protection running through the tariff of this country. We propose to light for it wherever we have the opportunity, and we do not propose to be diverted from it by insinuations as to our motives by such an hon. member as the representative for Brandon.

I have no intention of replying to the statements made by the hon. member (Mr. Stevens). Hon. members know me; they know all about me so far as that is concerned, and they are able to judge for themselves. He made one statement to which

I want to take exception. He said that I go outside the House and impugn the morality of members in that part of the chamber. I defy the hon. gentleman to find in any speech or any remarks that I have made at any time any words that ever imputed wrong motives to hon. gentlemen in that part of the House. What I have said, I have said on the floor of this House. I have often been found fault with because I have not used stronger language, because I have not been bitter enough against my hon. friends. In my own locality they will tell you that I am not bitter enough. I have paid tribute time and and time again to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mcighen), and newspapers have come out in the West with the heading "Forke lauds the leader of the opposition." That has occurred time and again, and yet hon. gentlemen in this House to-night say that I have impugned the morality of hon. members in that part cf the chamber. I deny it. I never used any language of that kind. [DOT]

It is only fair to the leader of the Progressive party to say that when he crossed the floor this afternoon, it was to ask me if a certain item that he pointed to in the Customs Act was free from the sales tax. That is the only conversation we had.
My hon. friend addressed a question to me some time ago and I think it has been lost sight of.
We have gone far afield.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

My hon. friend
says: "hear, hear." He must recognize that there is a time for justifiable anger. I have seen him very angry at very much smaller things. He used to have a dreadful way of being angry when he sat on this side. If you could only have seen my hon. friend perform at top speed when he was in opposition-I am sure he could have been heard on Sparks street-you would know what either real or simulated anger was. The acting minister asked me to withdraw this motion. It is perfectly true that while my hon. friend made the speech which I have read and which, I think, he will agree with me more than justifies everything that I am suggesting to-night, he did not press it to a motion. It is also true that what my hon. friend then wanted was to have lumber made entirely free. He was attacking a 3 per cent tax and nothing would satisfy him but absolutely free lumber. All I suggest is that he go back to the tax which he attacked. Three per cent was entirely too high then, but 5 per cent is
reasonable now. My hon. friend says he has given other concessions to the farmers and therefore I should not press the point. Now, one of the things I dislike about the whole of this budget, and the entire manner in which the sales tax exemptions are arrived at, is the total lack of anything like principle, the utter lack of any motive, except apparently that of expediency: whoever shouts the loudest and longest or can make the most trouble will get something. For the life of me I cannot see any justification in a scheme of sales taxation that exempts in part luxuries-and there are luxuries exempted here-and not only retains but even multiplies the tax on a common necessity of everybody, namely, lumber, to the taxation of which my hon. friend formerly objected. At the time the former tax was in effect the general field of taxation was infinitely broader than it is now; lots of things that were taxable then along with lumber were far less necessary than this article. And to the degree in which my hon. friend has exempted these other commodities, for which there is less justification for exemptions than in the case of lumber, just to that degree is the case for this particular exemption all the more strengthened. Fancy biscuits and the like are to be exempted from taxation; but what about this underlying national necessity? All I ask the minister to do is to put it where it was before; not to do what he says, namely, put it on the free list, but leave it where it was formerly. But, says my hon. friend, he cannot do that on account of the revenue. Well, if he pays attention to the hon. member for Brome and that gentleman's arguments with reference to the old tax, he will put this article back where it was and make more money. He will do that if the whole trouble is the revenue. And the trade will thank him for doing so. The trade know that (here is a great deal of difference between the three and the five per cent, and the trade will take a chance.

Does the hon. member say that the trade would rather go back to the old tax of 3 per cent than have the 5 per cent tax? If he says so he has been misinformed, because the manufacturers, the wholesalers and the retailers of this country are in favour of the present tax, and I know what I am speaking of.

There is no
doubt that the wholesaler and the jobber got what they wanted.

And the manufacturer.

It will cost the consumer

That tax was repeated and

I took the matter up with

The hon. member ought to

Surely there should be no debate on that score; there should be no idea of misrepresenting the law as it actually is:
Provided that in respect of lumber an excise tax of 3 per cent shall be imposed, levied and collected on sales and deliveries by the Canadian manufacturer, and further excise tax will not be payable on re-sale.
Now, that is the law to which I want to go back in the case of lumber. What idle nonsense it is to talk about duplication in connection with the motion which I have submitted in respect to lumber! What nonsense it is to refer to the evidence of Mr. Pedlow, who never mentioned lumber at all! What nonsense it is to say that three is greater than five-for that is what is being said!

4.	Resolved, That it is expedient to amend The Special War Revenue Act, 1915, and amending acts as follows, that is to say:	,
(a)	By repealing subsection three of section nineteen BBB of the said act and substituting therefor a new subsection three providing that if at any time it appears to the Minister of Customs and Excise that payment of the consumption or sales tax is being evaded by a licensed manufacturer or producer or licensed wholesaler or jobber the minister may require that the consumption or sales tax shall be imposed, levied and collected on any material specified by. the minister sold to any licensed manufacturer or producer or licensed wholesaler or jobber or to any class
of licensed manufacturers or producers or licensed wholesalers or jobbers specified by the minister, at the time of sale of such material when produced or manufactured in Canada, or at the time of entry for consumption by such licensed manufacturer or producer or licensed wholesaler or jobber when such material is imported, subject to deduction thereafter on submission by the licensed manufacturer or producer or licensed wholesaler or jobber of proof that such material has been used in the manufacture of an article which is subject to the consumption or sales tax and on which the said tax has been paid.
(b)	By repealing subsection five of said section nineteen BBB.
(c)	By striking out subsection six of said section nineteen BBB and substituting therefor the following:
" (6) Subject to the provisions of subsection three of this section, every manufacturer or producer shall take out an annual license for the purpose aforesaid, and the minister may prescribe a fee therefor, not exceeding two dollars, and the penalty for neglect shall be a sum not exceeding one thousand dollars. Provided that the minister may direct that any class of small manufacturer or producer selling his product exclusively by retail shall be exempt from payment of consumption or sales tax on goods manufactured or produced by him and persons so exempted shall not be given a license. Such exemption may be withdrawn by the minister."

In connection with this resolution, Mr. Chairman, I want to make this statement:
The section is designed essentially to protect the revenue. If evasion occurs in scattered individual cases the section would be invoked only in such cases, but if in any particular branch or class of industry there should appear widespread evasion, the section provides power for dealing with such cases as a "class." It may be and it is to be hoped that no occasion would ever arise for invoking the section as to a class or classes of industry, but it is felt desirable, in order to facilitate administration, that power should be given to deal with widespread evasion in a general way. Further, it may be that the nature of a particular line of business lends itself to evasions, and in such a case the only effective safeguard to the revenue would be to deal with the class and not the individual. But the committee may rest assured that the section will certainly not be invoked to cause hardship to the innocent majority on account of evasions by one or a few of their class.
This statement is given to me by the officers of the excise department, who have had experience in administering the act.

I am very glad my hon. friend has made the statement. Perhaps he will be able to go a little further. Perfectly reputable merchants have written to me in connection with the matter, and their point is very simple. They say that if a merchant offends he should be dealt with at once. But what they object to very strongly is that the whole of a decent trade should be

stigmatized and treated in this way because there happen to be one or two unscrupulous people engaged in it. It does make business infinitely more difficult to carry on, as my hon. friend well knows. I quite agree that he must protect the revenue, but instead of penalizing a whole class possibly-and I know the department will not want to do it, and simply because of their disinclination will render it all the more difficult to carry out the plan-I would suggest that an effective way to protect the revenue would be to make this offence of such a character that it would not be repeated; in other words, provide for very stringent penalties against offenders as individuals and not penalize a whole class, because perhaps 90 per cent of the class should not be penalized. It is a matter entirely for my hon. friend, and I am not going to say anything further. I agree with the object of the amendment, but I do not think it is at all wise to penalize in the omnibus way in which penalties can be inflicted under this section as amended.

I am satisfied that we can
trust the officers to use reasonable discretion. I do not think they would ever dare attack a class unless it was absolutely necessary.
Resolution as amended agreed to.

A refund of the consumption or sales tax may be granted on imported goods on which customs duties have been refunded on exportation; and a refund of the said tax may be granted on domestic goods exported, under regulations prescribed by the Minister of Customs and Excise.
